subject: DI02000121

intro_text.en: Unit 1 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121, Mechanical Semester 2, GTU 2024-25) lays the foundation of the whole subject: what mechanical drafting is and why industry runs on drawings, the drawing standards IS-696 / SP 46 (sheet sizes, title block, line types, scales), the four basic solids (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone) and how they are drawn, sectional views of solids, and development of surfaces for sheet-metal work. Everything in Units 2 to 7 - sections, GD&T, production and assembly drawings, and finally AutoCAD - is built on the line language and solids of this unit.

title.en: 1.1 Concept, need and standards of mechanical drafting
title.gu: 1.1 Concept, need and standards of mechanical drafting

h.en: 1.1 Concept and need of mechanical drafting
h.gu: 1.1 Concept and need of mechanical drafting

body.en:
What mechanical drafting is

Mechanical drafting is the preparation of engineering drawings of machine components and assemblies by standard conventions (projections, lines, symbols, dimensions and notes), so that a part designed by one person can be manufactured, inspected and assembled by others - anywhere, without the designer being present. The drawing is the complete technical definition of the product: it carries shape (views), size (dimensions), accuracy (tolerances/GD&T, Unit 3-4), surface quality (machining symbols), material and treatment (notes/title block) and joining methods (weld symbols). A component is never manufactured from an idea; it is manufactured from a drawing.

Why industry needs it (the rationale of this course)

  • Production: the workshop plans operations, selects machines, tools and process sequence (process planning) from the drawing.
  • Inspection and quality: inspectors verify the finished part against the same dimensions and tolerances printed on the drawing - the drawing is the acceptance document.
  • Assembly and maintenance: assembly drawings and the bill of materials tell what fits where, and in what quantity (Unit 5); spares are ordered by drawing/part number years later.
  • Estimation and purchasing: material, weight, standard bought-out parts (bolts, bearings) and cost are all read from drawings.
  • Legal/standard record: a signed, standardised drawing is a contract document between designer, manufacturer and customer; ambiguity is a defect, because every reader must extract exactly the same meaning.

Manual drafting plus CAD

This course builds manual sketching/sheet skills first (Practicals 1-6 on A2 sheets) and then the same drafting in AutoCAD (Units 6-7, Practical 7): the conventions never change - only the pencil becomes a mouse.

h.en: 1.1 Drawing standards: IS-696 / SP 46 - sheets, title block, lines and scales
h.gu: 1.1 Drawing standards: IS-696 / SP 46 - sheets, title block, lines and scales

body.en:
The standard

Indian drafting practice follows SP 46:1988 (Engineering Drawing Practice, BIS - successor to IS-696 practice). One standard used by every company is what makes a drawing readable across factories and countries.

Sheet sizes (trimmed, mm)

A0 = 841 x 1189, A1 = 594 x 841, A2 = 420 x 594, A3 = 297 x 420, A4 = 210 x 297. Each size is half the previous one. A border (10-20 mm) and filing margin are drawn inside; Practicals 1-6 of this course use A2 sheets. The title block (bottom-right, approx. 185 x 65 mm max) carries title, drawing number, scale, material, company, drawn/checked names with dates and revision - the identity card of the drawing (see diagram).

The alphabet of lines (learn this table)

  • Visible/object line - thick continuous: outlines and visible edges.
  • Hidden line - medium dashed: edges not visible in that view.
  • Centre line - thin long-short dash: axes of symmetry, circles, holes.
  • Cutting-plane line - thick long-short dash with arrows at ends: shows where the object is imagined cut (Unit 2).
  • Dimension, extension and Leader lines - thin continuous (Unit 7 in CAD; same convention manually).
  • Section (hatching) lines - thin, 45 deg, evenly spaced: cut material (Card 1.3).
  • Break line - thin freehand/zigzag: to show a long part partly.

Lettering and scales

All notes are in upright (or standard inclined) single-stroke capital lettering of standard heights (3.5/5/7 mm...). A drawing is made at a scale: full size (1:1), reducing scales (1:2, 1:5, 1:10...) for large parts, enlarging scales (2:1, 5:1) for tiny parts, expressed by the Representative Fraction RF = drawing size / actual size (1:2 means RF = 1/2). The scale used is always written in the title block - a photographically reduced print must never be scaled off with a ruler; only the written dimensions are worked to.

title.en: 1.2-1.3 Basic solids and their sectional views
title.gu: 1.2-1.3 Basic solids and their sectional views

h.en: 1.2 Basic solids: prism, pyramid, cylinder and cone
h.gu: 1.2 Basic solids: prism, pyramid, cylinder and cone

body.en:
The four basic solids (know their elements)

  • Prism: two equal parallel polygonal bases joined by rectangular faces (triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal prism...). Its axis joins the centres of the two bases. Machine examples: hexagonal bar stock, square keys, nuts (hexagonal prism with a hole).
  • Pyramid: a polygonal base with triangular faces meeting at an apex. Axis = line from apex to base centre. Examples: tool tips, conical-topped tanks (transition to cone), hopper bottoms.
  • Cylinder: two circular bases joined by a curved surface; generated by a rectangle rotating about one side (the axis). Examples: shafts, pipes, pins - the commonest solid in machinery.
  • Cone: a circular base and a slant (curved) surface meeting at the apex; generated by a right triangle rotating about one side. Slant height l = distance from apex to base rim along the surface. Examples: funnels, valves, tapered parts, bevel-gear blanks.

Vocabulary the examiner expects

Generator: any line on the surface through the apex (cone/pyramid) or parallel to the axis (cylinder/prism) - developments are built from generators. Right solid: axis perpendicular to base; oblique solid: axis inclined. Frustum: the remaining piece when the top of a cone/pyramid is cut off by a plane parallel to the base.

Drawing a solid = projecting it

A solid is drawn by its orthographic views (front view FV, top view TV, side view SV) in the standard positions: axis perpendicular to HP (standing on HP: e.g. cylinder = rectangle in FV, circle in TV), axis parallel to both planes, axis inclined, etc. Rules of projection never change: FV and TV are vertically aligned (same projector), lengths in FV/TV agree, heights in FV/SV agree. Practical 1 trains exactly these drawings - start with the view that shows the base shape (the circle/polygon), project the other view from it.

h.en: 1.3 Sectional views of basic solids and their applications
h.gu: 1.3 Sectional views of basic solids and their applications

body.en:
What a section of a solid shows

When a cutting plane slices a solid, the cut face is a plane figure - the true shape of section - and the remaining solid is drawn with the cut surface hatched. For basic solids the section shapes follow fixed geometry: a cylinder cut parallel to its axis gives a rectangle, perpendicular gives a circle, inclined gives an ellipse; a cone gives the conic sections - circle (plane parallel to base), ellipse (inclined, cutting all generators), parabola (parallel to one generator), hyperbola (steeper, cutting both nappes) and triangle (through the axis) - see diagram.

Why sections matter for solids themselves

  • Hollow solids: pipes, sleeves and hollow castings can only be defined by sectioning - wall thickness is invisible otherwise.
  • True shapes: sheet-metal and fabrication work needs the true shape of cut faces (branch pipes, truncated cones/frustums in ducts) - got from sectional views plus development (Card 1.4).
  • Foundation for Unit 2: sectioning a solid is the same operation as sectioning a machine part - cutting plane, hatching rules and removed/remaining half - practised here on simple geometry first.

Drawing routine

Draw the uncut views lightly, mark the cutting plane (cutting-plane line with arrows showing viewing direction, letters A-A), project the cut points onto the other view, join in order, hatch the cut material at 45 deg, and darken the final outlines. The cut surface is always behind the cutting plane on the side the arrows point away from - the nearer half is imagined removed.

title.en: 1.4 Development of surfaces and their uses
title.gu: 1.4 Development of surfaces and their uses

h.en: 1.4 Surface development of solids and their uses in engineering
h.gu: 1.4 Surface development of solids and their uses in engineering

body.en:
Principle

Development of a surface is the exact flat pattern obtained by unfolding/unrolling the solid's surface onto a plane, every edge and generator at its true length. Cut a sheet to this pattern, fold or roll it, and the solid is obtained - this is how sheet-metal and fabrication shops actually make parts.

Methods by solid (one per family)

  • Parallel-line method (prisms and cylinders): the surface is wrapped by parallel generators - development is a rectangle/strip whose one side = perimeter of base (for a cylinder, pi x D) and the other = height/length; base circles/polygons are attached separately (diagram).
  • Radial-line method (pyramids and cones): all generators radiate from the apex - development is a sector of a circle of radius = slant height l, with sector angle theta = (r / l) x 360 deg for a cone, where r = base radius (Numerical 1.1); for pyramids, true-length edges are laid out one face at a time around the apex.
  • Triangulation method (transition pieces, oblique and combination solids - the syllabus includes combinations of basic solids): the surface is divided into triangles, each drawn at true size.

Engineering uses

Ducts and chutes (square-to-round transitions), hoppers and bins, boiler and tank shells, chimneys, funnels, oil tanks, aircraft and automobile sheet panels, packaging cartons - all start as developments, with small allowances added for bending, seams and welding. Accuracy rule: use true lengths only (from the view where the edge/generator appears in true length, or construct it), because a development made from foreshortened lengths produces a part that will not close.

h.en: Practical 1: Draw basic solids and their sectional views
h.gu: Practical 1: Draw basic solids and their sectional views

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 1)

Draw basic solids (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone) in standard positions and draw their sectional views - first in the sketchbook, then on the A2 drawing sheet.

Instruments

A2 sheet/sketchbook, drawing board, mini-drafter or T-square, set squares, compass, scale, 0.5 mm H and 2H pencils, protractor (as per the official laboratory resources).

Procedure

  • Step 1: For each assigned solid and position (e.g., hexagonal prism standing on HP; cone with axis parallel to VP), draw the view showing the base shape first.
  • Step 2: Project the second view from it on the same projectors; check alignment (FV above TV in first-angle practice used in the laboratory).
  • Step 3: Apply the given cutting plane (e.g., axial vertical plane through a hollow cylinder), project cut points, and draw the sectional view with 45 deg hatching.
  • Step 4: Dimension the base size, height and cutting-plane position; add the title and scale in the title block.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet with all solids drawn, sections hatched, and a note naming each section shape obtained (rectangle/ellipse/triangle...). Conclusion: state which view shows the true shape of the base and of the section, and one error you corrected (misaligned projector, wrong hatch spacing, etc.).

h.en: Practical 2: Draw development of solid surfaces
h.gu: Practical 2: Draw development of solid surfaces

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 2)

Draw the development of the surfaces of basic solids (and simple combinations) - sketchbook first, then A2 sheet.

Principle

Parallel-line method for prisms/cylinders, radial-line for pyramids/cones (Card 1.4). Every edge in the development must be a true length.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Draw FV and TV of the solid; divide the base/circle into 12 equal parts and draw the generators.
  • Step 2: Lay out the development beside the views, transferring generator lengths from the view that shows them in true length.
  • Step 3: Join the points by straight lines (prism/pyramid) or a smooth curve (cylinder/cone); close the pattern with seam edge.
  • Step 4: Verify by calculation (cylinder strip length = pi x D; cone sector angle = (r/l) x 360 deg) and mark the check on the sheet.

Result (report format)

Submit pattern drawings with calculations shown. Optional suggested activity: cut the development in thick paper/sheet and fold it into the solid; attach a photograph or the folded model. Conclusion: name the method used for each solid and where such developments are used in the workshop.

h.en: Q1. What is mechanical drafting? Explain its need in industry.
h.gu: Q1. What is mechanical drafting? Explain its need in industry.

body.en:
Model answer

Mechanical drafting is the preparation of engineering drawings of machine parts and assemblies using standard conventions - projections, line types, symbols, dimensions, tolerances and notes - so that a component can be manufactured, inspected and assembled exactly as designed, by anyone, anywhere. It is needed because the drawing is the sole complete definition of the product: the workshop plans machining operations and process sheets from it; inspection accepts or rejects parts against its dimensions and tolerances; assembly drawings with the bill of materials control how parts fit together and in what numbers; estimation, purchasing of standard parts and costing are all read from it; and the signed drawing remains the legal record between designer, manufacturer and customer. Standardisation (SP 46) guarantees every trained reader extracts the same meaning, which is why drafting is called the language of engineers.

h.en: Q2. State the sheet sizes as per SP 46 and the contents of a title block.
h.gu: Q2. State the sheet sizes as per SP 46 and the contents of a title block.

body.en:
Model answer

Trimmed sheet sizes: A0 = 841 x 1189 mm, A1 = 594 x 841, A2 = 420 x 594, A3 = 297 x 420, A4 = 210 x 297 - each size half of the previous. The title block sits at the bottom-right corner of the sheet and contains: name/title of the component or assembly, drawing number, scale used, material, name of the company/institution, names and signatures of the persons who drew, checked and approved it with dates, sheet number, and revision information. It is the identity card of the drawing: a sheet without a filled title block is incomplete, because scale and material cannot be assumed from the picture.

h.en: Q3. Name the basic solids and define: generator, axis, apex, frustum.
h.gu: Q3. Name the basic solids and define: generator, axis, apex, frustum.

body.en:
Model answer

The basic solids of this course are the prism (two equal parallel polygonal bases joined by rectangular faces), the pyramid (polygonal base, triangular faces meeting at a point), the cylinder (two circular bases with a curved surface) and the cone (circular base with a slant surface). A generator is any straight line on the surface of the solid - through the apex for cone/pyramid, parallel to the axis for cylinder/prism. The axis is the line joining the centres of the two bases (prism/cylinder) or the apex to the base centre (pyramid/cone). The apex is the point where the triangular/slant faces of a pyramid/cone meet, opposite the base. A frustum is the part of a cone or pyramid that remains after the top is cut off by a plane parallel to the base.

h.en: Q4. Explain the parallel-line and radial-line methods of development with one application each.
h.gu: Q4. Explain the parallel-line and radial-line methods of development with one application each.

body.en:
Model answer

In the parallel-line method (prisms and cylinders) the lateral surface unrolls into a rectangle: one side equals the perimeter of the base (pi x D for a cylinder) and the other equals the height, because all generators are parallel and of equal length; it is used for pipes, tanks and rectangular ducts. In the radial-line method (pyramids and cones) all generators radiate from the apex, so the development is a sector of a circle whose radius is the slant height l and whose arc equals the base circumference; for a cone the sector angle theta = (r/l) x 360 deg. It is used for funnels, conical hoppers and reducers. In both methods only true lengths may be transferred, otherwise the folded part will not close.

h.en: Q5. List any six types of lines used in engineering drawing with their applications.
h.gu: Q5. List any six types of lines used in engineering drawing with their applications.

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Visible line - thick continuous, for outlines and visible edges. (2) Hidden line - medium dashes, for edges not visible in the view. (3) Centre line - thin long-and-short dashes, for axes of holes, shafts and symmetrical features. (4) Cutting-plane line - thick long-short dashes ending in arrows, to show the plane of section and viewing direction. (5) Dimension/extension/Leader lines - thin continuous, to write sizes. (6) Section lines - thin lines at 45 deg, to hatch cut material in sectional views. (Any six standard types earn the marks; the diagram md1_lines shows all of them.)

(4) Cutting-plane line - thick long-short dashes ending in arrows, to show the plane of section and viewing direction. (5) Dimension/extension/Leader lines - thin continuous, to write sizes. (6) Section lines - thin lines at 45 deg, to hatch cut material in sectional views. (Any six standard types earn the marks; the diagram md1_lines shows all of them.)

h.en: Q6. What is development of a surface? State its engineering uses.
h.gu: Q6. What is development of a surface? State its engineering uses.

body.en:
Model answer

Development of a surface is the exact flat pattern of a solid's surface obtained by unfolding it on a plane with every edge and generator at true length. Uses: sheet-metal products such as ducts, chutes and square-to-round transition pieces; hoppers, bins and funnels; cylindrical tanks, boiler shells and chimneys; and any fabricated part that is cut flat and then bent or rolled into shape. The development, with bending and seam allowances added, is directly the cutting layout for the sheet.

h.en: Q7. A cone is cut by different planes. Name the section obtained in each case.
h.gu: Q7. A cone is cut by different planes. Name the section obtained in each case.

body.en:
Model answer

Plane parallel to the base: circle. Plane inclined to the axis cutting all generators: ellipse. Plane parallel to one generator: parabola. Plane inclined more steeply, cutting the axis at a smaller angle than the generators (through both nappes of a double cone): hyperbola. Plane passing through the axis: triangle (isosceles, equal to the axial section). These are the conic sections; the same list with 'rectangle/circle/ellipse' applies to the cylinder for planes parallel/perpendicular/inclined to its axis.

h.en: Q8. Define scale and Representative Fraction. A part 200 mm long is drawn 100 mm long; find the scale.
h.gu: Q8. Define scale and Representative Fraction. A part 200 mm long is drawn 100 mm long; find the scale.

body.en:
Model answer

Scale is the ratio between the size of an object on the drawing and its actual size. Representative Fraction (RF) = size on drawing / actual size, both in the same units. Here RF = 100/200 = 1/2, so the scale is 1:2 (a reducing scale - the drawing is half full size). Full-size drawings have RF = 1 (1:1); enlarging scales such as 2:1 have RF = 2. The scale is always stated in the title block, and sizes must be taken from written dimensions, never measured off a printed sheet.

title.en: Numerical 1.1 - Development of a cone (sector angle and pattern size)
title.gu: Numerical 1.1 - Development of a cone (sector angle and pattern size)

body.en:
Given

A right cone has base diameter 60 mm and height 40 mm. Its lateral surface is to be developed for a sheet-metal funnel.

Find

Slant height, sector angle of the development, and the minimum square sheet size that contains the pattern.

Formula

Slant height l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2) ; sector angle theta = (r / l) x 360 deg ; sector arc must equal base circumference 2 x pi x r

Substitution and calculation

r = 30 mm ; l = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(2500) = 50 mm
theta = (30 / 50) x 360 = 216 deg
Check arc: (216/360) x 2 x pi x 50 = 188.5 mm ; base circumference = 2 x pi x 30 = 188.5 mm [OK]
Pattern radius = l = 50 mm; the 216 deg sector fits in a square of about 100 x 100 mm
Development: sector of radius 50 mm and angle 216 deg (base circle of dia. 60 mm attached separately)

Validity check

The arc-length equality is the governing check of every radial-line development - if the two numbers differ, the funnel will not close at the seam.

title.en: Numerical 1.2 - Development of a cylindrical tank shell (sheet size)
title.gu: Numerical 1.2 - Development of a cylindrical tank shell (sheet size)

body.en:
Given

A closed cylindrical vessel of diameter 50 mm and height 80 mm is made from sheet.

Find

Size of the rectangle for the curved surface and the total sheet area including both circular ends (ignore seam allowances).

Formula

Development of curved surface = rectangle of (pi x D) x H ; end area = (pi/4) x D^2 each

Substitution and calculation

Length = pi x 50 = 157.1 mm ; rectangle = 157.1 x 80 mm
Curved area = 157.1 x 80 = 12,566 mm2
Two ends = 2 x (pi/4) x 50^2 = 2 x 1963.5 = 3927 mm2
Total sheet = 12,566 + 3927 = 16,493 mm2
Cut a 157.1 mm x 80 mm rectangle for the shell plus two dia. 50 mm circles; total approx. 16,493 mm2 of sheet

Validity check

Units mm and mm2 consistent; the rectangle length must be pi x D (not D) - using the diameter directly is the commonest first-year error in this calculation.

title.en: Practical 1: Draw basic solids and their sectional views
title.gu: Practical 1: Draw basic solids and their sectional views

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 1)

Draw basic solids (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone) in standard positions and draw their sectional views - first in the sketchbook, then on the A2 drawing sheet.

Instruments

A2 sheet/sketchbook, drawing board, mini-drafter or T-square, set squares, compass, scale, 0.5 mm H and 2H pencils, protractor (as per the official laboratory resources).

Procedure

  • Step 1: For each assigned solid and position (e.g., hexagonal prism standing on HP; cone with axis parallel to VP), draw the view showing the base shape first.
  • Step 2: Project the second view from it on the same projectors; check alignment (FV above TV in first-angle practice used in the laboratory).
  • Step 3: Apply the given cutting plane (e.g., axial vertical plane through a hollow cylinder), project cut points, and draw the sectional view with 45 deg hatching.
  • Step 4: Dimension the base size, height and cutting-plane position; add the title and scale in the title block.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet with all solids drawn, sections hatched, and a note naming each section shape obtained (rectangle/ellipse/triangle...). Conclusion: state which view shows the true shape of the base and of the section, and one error you corrected (misaligned projector, wrong hatch spacing, etc.).

title.en: Practical 2: Draw development of solid surfaces
title.gu: Practical 2: Draw development of solid surfaces

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 2)

Draw the development of the surfaces of basic solids (and simple combinations) - sketchbook first, then A2 sheet.

Principle

Parallel-line method for prisms/cylinders, radial-line for pyramids/cones (Card 1.4). Every edge in the development must be a true length.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Draw FV and TV of the solid; divide the base/circle into 12 equal parts and draw the generators.
  • Step 2: Lay out the development beside the views, transferring generator lengths from the view that shows them in true length.
  • Step 3: Join the points by straight lines (prism/pyramid) or a smooth curve (cylinder/cone); close the pattern with seam edge.
  • Step 4: Verify by calculation (cylinder strip length = pi x D; cone sector angle = (r/l) x 360 deg) and mark the check on the sheet.

Result (report format)

Submit pattern drawings with calculations shown. Optional suggested activity: cut the development in thick paper/sheet and fold it into the solid; attach a photograph or the folded model. Conclusion: name the method used for each solid and where such developments are used in the workshop.
